newsitem.title: USA: Heinz, Campbell Soup settle employee dispute.
newsitem.headline: Heinz, Campbell Soup settle employee dispute.

text.p: H.J. Heinz Co. and Campbell Soup Co. said Thursday they were ending their food fight over Daniel O'Neill, a former top Campbell executive hired by Heinz, and both sides claimed victory.
The settlement ended what had become a bitter legal battle over O'Neill.
The spat began Jan. 6, when Heinz hired O'Neill away from Campbell, which challenged the move as a violation of an 18-month non-compete agreement O'Neill signed.
Under the settlement, O'Neill will be able to resume his duties at Heinz in seven months, on Sept. 15. He will remain on the payroll during the period, a Heinz spokesman said.
Until September, O'Neill is prohibited from having business contacts with Heinz and its employees.
O'Neill can have social contact with directors and employees of the Pittsburgh-based company but will be prohibited from social events where Heinz business may be discussed in his presence.

Heinz spokesman Edward Smyth said allowing O'Neill to have social contacts was an important issue in the settlement, and it would be no problem for O'Neill to keep his business and social lives separate.
"It would be a very boring company that couldn't have a dinner party and not talk about business for an evening," he said.
O'Neill, president of Camden, N.J.-based Campbell's U.S. soup and prepared foods division, was tapped in January to be executive vice president of Heinz's pet food and Star-Kist tuna operations.
Heinz said the job would not compete with Campbell business, but Campbell challenged the hiring in federal court.
Heinz is known for ketchup, pickles and other food products. It competes with Campbell as a major maker of private-label soup and in other areas.

O'Neill had first been offered a job as head of Heinz brands in North America. This raised concerns he was hired for the pet-food job only as a way of avoiding the non-compete terms, Campbell spokesman Kevin Lowery said.

"It struck a nerve here," Lowery said. "To have someone who was part of the family jump ship over to our No. 1 competitor ... number one, we felt like we had to protect the company's assets, and number two, we felt violated."
The settlement, he said, "shows that our non-compete agreements have teeth."
Said Heinz President William Johnson in a statement, "This agreement is a victory for common sense."
"A seven-month hiatus in the context of Dan's expected 20-year career at Heinz is of no consequence," he said.
The agreement says O'Neill will be free to assume "wider responsibilities" at Heinz on Aug. 12, 1998, but Heinz did not say what they might be.

The settlement also requires O'Neill to maintain until August 1998 -- 18 months from the settlement day -- meticulous daily logs of all his business meetings and discussions, which would be reviewed for compliance by an outside auditor.
In addition, it also allows for an independent engineer to inspect Heinz manufacturing facilities to ensure no Campbell manufacturing secrets are taken.
In leaving Campbell, O'Neill will give up $1.4 million in compensation and benefits.

His package at Heinz included a $1 million signing bonus and options to buy 500,000 shares of Heinz stock. Under the settlement, the 400,000 options that would have been exerciseable immediately were extended to the year 2000.
After the settlement, sniping continued between the two food giants.

Heinz spokesman Smyth compared hammering out the settlment to "dealing with the Stalinists in the old days," and said his company didn't need non-compete agreements to retain employees. "We use good morale and stock options to keep our people," he said.
Campbell spokesman Lowery, referring to the period of O'Neill's restricted activity, said, "If they (Heinz) want to pay somebody to sit around, that's up to them."
On the New York Stock Exchange, Campbell stock bubbled up 62.5 cents to $86.375, while 25 cents was squeezed out of Heinz, leaving it at $41.125.
